name: Tulsi (Holy Basil)
variety: Species identity; no tulsi type or cultivar specified
summary: Tulsi is the species Ocimum tenuiflorum, distinct from culinary sweet basil. NC State Extension describes its rapid multistem growth, aromatic foliage, variable flower colors, culinary leaf use and regional spread/pest cautions; no cultivar is specified.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ocimum tenuiflorum. North Carolina Extension lists Tulsi, Tulasi and Holy Basil as common names and notes the historical name O. sanctum. This is not an Ocimum basilicum cultivar.

growth.short: Aromatic, fast-growing upright herb with a multi-stem form
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes holy basil as an aromatic annual or short-lived perennial/subshrub, growing rapidly to about 3 feet with an erect, multi-stemmed form. Its opposite leaves are aromatic and may have a purple cast; stems can be green or purple. The source describes it as shorter-lived than culinary sweet basil; actual lifespan depends on conditions. These are species-level traits, not cultivar measurements.

cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes a rapidly growing, erect, multi-stemmed herb that prefers full sun and moist, well-drained soil, and recommends a confined area or container to manage spread. This is regional outdoor guidance; it does not establish an indoor lamp setting or hydroponic recipe.

propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed propagation and notes that the plant readily self-seeds. Exact sowing depth, germination time and temperature are not supplied in the reviewed page.

harvest.guidance: NC State Extension describes the leaves as a culinary herb, commonly cooked or used in teas. It distinguishes their spicy flavor from ordinary culinary basil; this is species-level guidance.

problems.guidance: The extension profile notes self-seeding and potential weediness outside the native range; contain plants where unwanted spread is a concern. It also reports Japanese beetles skeletonizing leaves and recommends hand removal. This is a regional source warning, not a claim that the pest or invasive behavior occurs everywhere.

flowering.short: Small flowers form in terminal clusters; color varies
flowering.guidance: NC State Extension describes small tubular flowers in terminal racemes or panicles, with white, pink or purple reported across the species account. This is a species-level color range, not a prediction for an unnamed cultivar or an indoor bloom guarantee.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The reviewed sources do not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: Species-level growth habit described by NC State Extension.
Extension reports growth to about 3 ft; only the reported upper size is represented.

name: Common Fenugreek
variety: Species identity; no named cultivar specified
summary: Common fenugreek is the annual species Trigonella foenum-graecum, grown for its foliage and mature seeds. NC State describes the species, while OMAFRA adds regional Ontario field-production and harvest context; no named cultivar or hydroponic recipe is represented.

metrics.label: Mature height
metrics.note: Species-level outdoor range · NC State Extension

metrics.label: Herb harvest
metrics.note: Ontario crop guidance; not a universal home-garden countdown · OMAFRA

metrics.label: Seed production
metrics.note: Ontario crop guidance; distinct from leaf harvest · OMAFRA

identity.guidance: Kew accepts this annual species in Fabaceae. Fenugreek, Greek clover and Greek hay are common names; no cultivar or production type is inferred.

cultivation.short: Full sun; avoid persistently wet soil
cultivation.guidance: North Carolina Extension lists full sun and good drainage. OMAFRA describes fenugreek production in Ontario at 18–27°C, in well-drained loamy soil, and notes vegetative-stage frost tolerance; these are field-crop conditions, not an indoor or hydroponic prescription.

growth.short: Erect annual with compound foliage and seed pods
growth.guidance: NC State describes an erect, rapidly growing annual about 1 ft 3 in–2 ft tall. Its oval leaflets can reach about 2 in and are hairy underneath; small flowers appear in upper leaf axils, followed by pointed pods up to 4 in long with roughly 10–20 seeds. These are species-level descriptions, not a named cultivar profile.
items: A mature plant may be recognized by its compound foliage and elongated seed pods.
The source reports summer flowering and summer-to-fall harvest context; it does not establish a fixed local calendar.

propagation.guidance: NC State and OMAFRA identify seed as a propagation route. Detailed sowing, seed handling and germination evidence is kept in the linked Seed Profile rather than duplicated in established-plant care.

harvest.short: Leaf harvest and seed production follow different schedules
harvest.guidance: NC State describes green plant parts as an herb/spice and mature seeds as a condiment. In Ontario production guidance, OMAFRA gives 30–40 days for herb harvest and 105–140 days for seed production, with earlier summer herb harvest sometimes needed to avoid flowering. These are regional crop ranges, not a universal home-garden countdown or named-cultivar promise.

problems.short: Wet soils are a documented concern
problems.guidance: NC State warns that wet soils are unsuitable. OMAFRA's limited Ontario crop observations include leafhoppers, tarnished plant bug, Alternaria leaf spot and root rot; it is a regional observation list, not a complete pest inventory or a diagnosis for an individual plant. OMAFRA notes good site selection and airflow as disease-pressure considerations.

care.short: Cool-season crop; avoid overwatering and keep drainage open
care.guidance: UC Master Gardeners describe fenugreek as a cool-season herb with low-to-moderate water needs and good drainage, advising against overwatering. OMAFRA says irrigation benefits herb production under Ontario conditions. Keep those regional recommendations in context; neither source defines a fixed indoor watering schedule.

flowering.short: Leaf harvest and seed production have different flowering goals
flowering.guidance: UC Master Gardeners describe fenugreek as a cool-season herb that begins to set seed as spring temperatures warm and advise allowing regrowth and flowers when seed is the goal. OMAFRA notes that herb harvest may need to happen earlier in hot weather to avoid flowering. This is a crop-purpose decision, not a universal instruction to remove every flower.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The reviewed sources describe soil cultivation and do not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: Species-level habit from NC State Extension.
Converted from 1 ft 3 in–2 ft reported by NC State.

spacing.reason: The source gives a broad available-space range, not a selected universal spacing.

name: Peppermint
variety: Accepted horticultural hybrid; no cultivar specified
summary: Peppermint is the accepted hybrid Mentha × piperita, distinct from spearmint (M. spicata) and from the existing broad Common Mint record. NC State documents rhizomatous spread and recommends vegetative propagation.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Mentha × piperita and gives the hybrid formula M. aquatica × M. spicata. It is not interchangeable with the species Mentha spicata or the unresolved broad Common Mint identity.

growth.short: Upright, fast-growing perennial that spreads by rhizomes
growth.guidance: NC State describes peppermint as an upright perennial hybrid that forms an aggressive groundcover through rhizomes. Its reported height and spread are outdoor regional ranges, not container or indoor-system guarantees.

cultivation.guidance: NC State describes an upright, rhizomatous perennial that prefers rich, moist soil and partial shade in its regional context. It spreads aggressively; the source suggests container culture as a way to contain the plant, not as a hydroponic recommendation.

propagation.short: Vegetative propagation is the recommended route
propagation.guidance: NC State lists division and stem cuttings as propagation strategies and notes that the plant rarely sets seed. Use vegetative material when preserving the selected hybrid identity; the source does not establish seed-starting instructions.

harvest.short: Leaves and flowers have culinary uses
harvest.guidance: NC State lists fresh or dried leaves and flowers for teas, beverages, sauces and other uses, and reports pinching as a way to encourage bushier growth. Johnny's general Mentha guide says individual leaves can be picked once plants are established, while a whole-plant harvest is timed just before flowering; for drying, it recommends a warm, well-ventilated place out of direct sun. The harvest timing and drying method are genus-level crop guidance, not a peppermint-specific yield or essential-oil rule.

pruning.short: Pinch branch tips to encourage bushier, leafier growth
pruning.guidance: NC State recommends regularly pinching branch tips; it says this promotes bushier, leafier growth and increases available harvest. This is established-plant management, not a seedling protocol.

flowering.short: Small pink-to-lavender flowers bloom in summer; seed is rarely set
flowering.guidance: NC State describes small tubular pink-to-lavender flowers in dense terminal spikes, blooming in summer. It reports that peppermint rarely sets seed, consistent with treating Mentha × piperita as a hybrid usually maintained vegetatively. This is North Carolina source context, not a universal bloom calendar.

problems.guidance: NC State characterizes peppermint as an aggressive rhizomatous ground cover and lists low-severity poison characteristics: large human ingestions may cause vomiting or diarrhea, and the plant is flagged as a problem for cats, dogs, and horses. Contain its spread and keep access by pets in mind. This warning does not turn culinary leaf use into a medicinal claim or provide a dose; concentrated essential oils are not interchangeable with culinary leaves.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No cited source establishes peppermint performance in nutrient-solution hydroponics.

evidence.note: Hybrid is described as upright and rhizomatous/spreading.
Converted from NC State's 1–3 ft range.
NC State gives a 1–2 ft spread and separately warns of aggressive rhizomatous spread; context is outdoor general.

spacing.reason: Soil spacing does not establish pod or indoor spacing.

evidence.note: Full sun and partial shade are both listed outdoor options; neither is mapped to an indoor grow-light requirement.

name: Wishbone Flower (Torenia)
variety: Species identity; violet color is not a named cultivar
summary: Torenia fournieri is the species-level identity supported for the reference name Torenia. North Carolina Extension documents seed propagation, container use, shade/part-sun conditions and pinching; a violet cultivar is not established.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Torenia fournieri in Linderniaceae. NC State uses Wishbone Flower as a common name and notes that many cultivars exist; the supplied violet color alone does not establish one.

cultivation.short: Shade and containers are documented options
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes part-sun to shade preference, especially in hot summers, and use in containers, hanging baskets and shade borders. It recommends rich, moist soil and mulch to keep roots cool. This is outdoor/container horticultural guidance, not proof of indoor-system compatibility.

growth.short: Low-growing annual with an upright-to-spreading habit
growth.guidance: NC State gives a broad species-page range of 6–18 inches tall and 6–8 inches wide. This is general Torenia fournieri guidance, not a dimension for an unidentified violet cultivar.

flowering.short: Two-tone trumpet flowers bloom through summer and fall
flowering.guidance: NC State describes a long bloom season with two-tone tubular flowers and a distinctive wishbone-shaped pair of stamens. The species page describes violet/blue tones, while many cultivars extend the color range; the violet reference name does not identify a cultivar.

propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed as a propagation strategy for the species. The selected source does not provide sowing depth, temperature or germination timing.

pruning.short: Pinching can retain a bushier form
pruning.guidance: NC State recommends pinching back to retain a bushier shape. The claim is species-level cultivation guidance and does not define a fixed pruning schedule.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Shade-garden/container suitability is not evidence for hydroponic compatibility.

evidence.note: Both habit forms are listed at species scope.

name: Alice Sundew
summary: Drosera aliciae is an accepted South African carnivorous perennial. RHS documents fresh-seed propagation, leaf/root cuttings, wet lime-free water and full-light cultivation; no conventional hydroponic compatibility is inferred.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Drosera aliciae. RHS lists the species as a perennial carnivorous plant native to the South African Cape; this identity is separate from Cape Sundew (D. capensis).

growth.short: Dense basal rosette that can form a low mound
growth.guidance: RHS describes spoon-shaped leaves with sticky red glands in a dense, clumping basal rosette. Older dead basal leaves can build into a 1.5–4 cm mound; RHS separately lists maximum plant height up to 10 cm and spread of 0.1–0.5 m. These are RHS profile dimensions, not a guaranteed indoor footprint.

cultivation.guidance: RHS describes cultivation under glass in full light, with medium kept continually moist to wet during the growing season using lime-free water; it advises less water standing in winter and no fertilizer. These species-specific carnivorous-plant conditions are not a nutrient-solution recipe.

flowering.short: Deep-pink flowers rise above the rosette in summer
flowering.guidance: RHS reports a summer inflorescence up to 4 cm tall, bearing 2–12 individual deep-pink flowers that open in ascending order. This describes normal flowering, not a signal that the rosette is failing.

pruning.guidance: RHS states that pruning is not required for Drosera aliciae. The profile does not prescribe removing healthy leaves or flower stalks.

propagation.short: Fresh seed and cuttings are documented
propagation.guidance: RHS recommends sowing seed as soon as ripe and notes that stored seed rapidly loses viability. Leaf cuttings in the growing season and root cuttings during dormancy are alternatives; no numeric germination schedule is reported.

problems.short: Avoid interpreting low mucilage without checking conditions
problems.guidance: SANBI describes the species as a carnivorous plant of moist conditions. Do not diagnose a problem from appearance alone; check the documented moisture and water-quality context before intervention.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Carnivorous-plant wet-media guidance does not establish recirculating hydroponic nutrient-solution suitability.

evidence.note: RHS describes a dense basal rosette and clumping/mounding habit.

height.reason: RHS dimensions are specifically under-glass and that context is not represented by Compatibility Profile v1; the sourced Plant Profile retains the reported size.

spread.reason: No supported mature spread was selected.

evidence.note: RHS says full light under glass; this does not describe outdoor sun exposure or a grow-light intensity tier.

name: Tennessee Coneflower
variety: Accepted species identity; not a cultivar of Echinacea purpurea
summary: Tennessee Coneflower is the accepted species Echinacea tennesseensis, not a Tennessee-selected cultivar of E. purpurea. Kew confirms its narrow native range; University of Tennessee guidance stresses isolation from other Echinacea when maintaining seed genetic integrity.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Echinacea tennesseensis and lists the historic combination E. angustifolia var. tennesseensis as a synonym. NC State also treats Tennessee Coneflower as the species name, not a cultivar of E. purpurea.

growth.short: Slow-growing perennial, about 1–2 ft tall and wide
growth.guidance: NC State reports a slow growth rate and a species-level landscape range of 1–2 ft in both height and width. This is outdoor garden information, not an indoor pod or machine-size estimate.

cultivation.short: Full sun to part shade; average moist-to-dry soils
cultivation.guidance: NC State reports full sun to part shade and average moist-to-dry soils in its regional plant guidance. Kew and NC State describe its native range as Tennessee; these landscape conditions do not establish hydroponic compatibility.

flowering.short: Distinctive erect pink-purple rays bloom June through August
flowering.guidance: NC State describes erect pink-purple ray flowers around an orange disk from June to August. Flowering is a normal seasonal stage; timing is regional, not an indoor schedule.

care.short: Keep seed source isolated from other Echinacea if preserving identity
care.guidance: NC State and University of Tennessee Extension warn that Echinacea tennesseensis cross-pollinates with other Echinacea; seed grown near other coneflowers may not remain true to type. UT guidance says isolation is needed when seed genetic integrity is the goal, but does not establish an exact distance. This is a seed-production caveat, not a routine pruning instruction.

propagation.short: Seed may require isolation to preserve identity
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed as a propagation route and warns that cross-pollination with other Echinacea can produce seed that does not grow true to type. University of Tennessee Extension also advises isolation for seed genetic integrity but gives no exact distance or household germination protocol; do not create a Seed Profile without that evidence.

uses.short: Border, meadow or woodland planting for pollinators and finches
uses.guidance: NC State lists border, meadow and woodland-garden use, and reports pollinator visits and finches eating the seeds. The source supports ornamental and wildlife value, not edible use by people.

problems.short: Japanese beetles are occasional; leaf spot is reported rarely
problems.guidance: NC State reports no serious recurring problems, with occasional Japanese beetles and rare leaf spot. These are source observations, not a claim of disease resistance.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No source reviewed establishes hydroponic suitability.

name: Micro-Tom Tomato
summary: Micro-Tom is a named dwarf, determinate tomato cultivar developed by the University of Florida. NParks describes a bushy plant about 15–20 cm tall with small red fruits borne in a concentrated set. UF research included Micro-Tom among compact cultivars studied indoors; that is not a universal hydroponic compatibility claim.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Solanum lycopersicum as the cultivated tomato species. NParks identifies Micro-Tom as a dwarf, determinate cultivar developed by the University of Florida; no claim is made that it is the same cultivar as Tiny Tim.

cultivation.short: Outdoor sun and container context are documented
cultivation.guidance: NParks recommends at least 4–6 hours of direct sun, lists container planting, and describes well-drained fertile loamy soil. UF research included Micro-Tom among compact tomato cultivars evaluated indoors. The outdoor sun figure is not an indoor grow-light tier, and the study does not establish universal hydroponic compatibility.

growth.short: Bushy, dwarf and determinate; compact fruit set
growth.guidance: NParks describes Micro-Tom as a bushy, dwarf, determinate cultivar reaching about 15–20 cm. Its round, deep-red fruits are about 1.5 cm wide, with roughly 25 fruits typically borne together. These are NParks cultivar-level observations, not dimensions or yield expectations for other dwarf tomatoes.

harvest.short: Use the red, smooth fruit cue; no dependable day-count is published
harvest.guidance: NParks describes Micro-Tom fruit as ripe when red and smooth, with a concentrated crop. Its page conflicts internally: narrative text says about 50–60 days from sowing, while a separate field lists 90–120 days to typical fruiting. Gardenpedia does not publish either as a reliable schedule; use the visible fruit cue and treat the exact timing as unknown.

care.short: Keep the root zone moist but free-draining; avoid a fixed watering rule
care.guidance: NParks lists both moderate and high water preferences and a well-drained, fertile loam root zone, so it does not establish one precise water amount. UMN's general tomato advice favors consistent soil moisture and watering at the base; use the medium and plant condition rather than a calendar or reservoir volume.

support.short: A compact determinate bush; routine trellising is not established as necessary
support.guidance: NParks identifies Micro-Tom as a dwarf, determinate, bushy cultivar. UMN says bush-type tomatoes generally do not need staking or trellising, but does not test Micro-Tom specifically; inspect the actual plant and fruit load instead of assuming a support system is never needed.

problems.short: Monitor listed sap-feeding pests and avoid overfeeding
problems.guidance: NParks lists aphids, whiteflies, red spider mites and root-knot nematodes as potential problems, and cautions that over-fertilising can encourage aphids. Check foliage regularly; this is a source-listed watchlist, not a diagnosis or a product-specific pesticide recommendation.

flowering.short: Flower movement supports fruit set; sustained heat can cause flower drop
flowering.guidance: At tomato crop level, UMN Extension explains that flower parts sit close together and flower movement can transfer pollen; tomatoes can produce fruit without bee pollination. UMN's Minnesota-specific example says sustained days above 85°F and nights above 70°F can stress flowers and impair fruit set; flowers may then drop. Treat this as regional context, not a Micro-Tom trial result or indoor setpoint.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: UF indoor compact-tomato research and cultivar size do not establish nutrient-solution compatibility or system-specific pod limits.

evidence.note: NParks describes Micro-Tom itself as a dwarf, determinate cultivar with a bushy growth habit.
NParks lists Micro-Tom maximum height as 15–20 cm; measurement context is unspecified, so the contract retains that context.

spacing.reason: No cultivar-specific spacing was selected; do not infer pod spacing from compact dimensions.

light.reason: Cultivar indoor-research presence does not provide a numeric or categorical light requirement.

name: Orange Hat Tomato
variety: Named cultivar/product identity 'Orange Hat'; supplier documentation scope
summary: Orange Hat is a separately marketed micro-dwarf tomato cultivar, distinct from Micro-Tom and Tiny Tim. Baker Creek describes its extra-dwarf habit, orange fruit and container care; those product-specific details are not generalized to tomato species.

identity.short: Named commercial cultivar identity: Orange Hat
identity.guidance: Kew accepts the species Solanum lycopersicum. Baker Creek sells Orange Hat tomato seed as a named product. Its supplier page is used for product/cultivar attributes only; no breeder or formal registration claim is made.

cultivation.short: Product is described for sunny windows or patio containers
cultivation.guidance: Baker Creek describes Orange Hat as an extra-dwarf, determinate bush, 6–9 inches tall, suited to patio/container growing and full sun. The supplier's sun statement is outdoor exposure; its separate mention of sunny windows and grow lights does not give an indoor light duration or prove universal hydroponic compatibility.

growth.short: Extra-dwarf determinate bush, listed at 6–9 inches
growth.guidance: Baker Creek describes its Orange Hat product as an extra-dwarf, determinate bush reaching 6–9 inches, with small orange fruits. These are seller-reported cultivar characteristics and should not be generalized to Micro-Tom, Tiny Tim or dwarf tomatoes as a group.

care.short: Regular watering and occasional balanced feeding; no schedule specified
care.guidance: Baker Creek recommends regular watering and occasional balanced fertilizer for Orange Hat, but gives no measured interval or dose. Iowa State notes that container tomatoes can dry quickly, need thorough watering with drainage and should not remain waterlogged; this general container guidance is not a hydroponic recipe.

support.short: Baker Creek says staking is not required for this compact product
support.guidance: The supplier states that Orange Hat's compact size does not require staking. Treat this as a product-level recommendation; inspect the actual plant if fruit load or growing conditions cause stems to lean.

harvest.guidance: Baker Creek lists 55–65 days to maturity and describes Orange Hat fruit as orange and sweet. The figure is a product estimate, not a guaranteed date or a clearly defined sowing-to-harvest interval; use full fruit color as a cue, with Iowa State's general tomato guidance that ripe fruit gives slightly to touch.

pruning.short: Heavy pruning is not advised by the supplier
pruning.guidance: Baker Creek says heavy pruning is unnecessary for this determinate cultivar and describes only light lower-leaf trimming. This is a supplier-specific recommendation, not a universal tomato rule.

problems.short: Watch for cracking or blossom-end rot when moisture fluctuates
problems.guidance: No Orange Hat-specific disease resistance or susceptibility is established here. Iowa State describes cracking and blossom-end rot as moisture-related issues in container tomatoes; inspect the fruit and growing medium before diagnosing, and do not treat these crop-level risks as a cultivar defect.

flowering.short: Flower movement supports fruit set; sustained heat can cause flower drop
flowering.guidance: At tomato crop level, UMN Extension explains that flower parts sit close together and flower movement can transfer pollen; tomatoes can produce fruit without bee pollination. UMN's Minnesota-specific example says sustained days above 85°F and nights above 70°F can stress flowers and impair fruit set; flowers may then drop. Treat this as regional context, not an Orange Hat trial result or indoor setpoint.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Supplier references windowsills and containers but do not establish hydroponic nutrient-solution performance.

height.reason: Cultivar-specific dimensions remain in sourced Plant Profile content; Compatibility Profile v1 does not encode cultivar-level evidence scope.

spacing.reason: Supplier's outdoor/container spacing is not a universal indoor pod-spacing recommendation.

light.reason: The supplier describes full sun but this is not normalized into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Black Pearl Ornamental Pepper
summary: Black Pearl is the USDA-released ornamental cultivar Capsicum annuum 'Black Pearl', selected for dark foliage and upright fruit clusters that mature from black to red. Its ornamental selection does not establish a culinary-use recommendation or hydroponic compatibility.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Capsicum annuum at species level. USDA ARS identifies Black Pearl as a named ornamental cultivar developed with the U.S. National Arboretum and PanAmerican Seed; it is not a generic black-fruited pepper type.

growth.short: Compact, upright annual; averages 18 in tall by 12 in wide
growth.guidance: The U.S. National Arboretum reports an average height of 18 inches and diameter of 12 inches; in warmer regions with longer growing seasons, plants may reach 2–3 feet tall. These are cultivar-specific outdoor garden measurements, not indoor-clearance or hydroponic-spacing specifications.

cultivation.short: Selected for ornamental foliage and fruit
cultivation.guidance: USDA ARS describes black foliage and upright clusters of small fruits that turn red, with compact ornamental performance and limited evaluation for pot culture under high light. The National Arboretum recommends full sun for best growth and black leaf color, and well-drained loam or sandy loam with some organic matter. Neither source establishes a general hydroponic protocol.

care.short: Compact shape does not require pruning
care.guidance: The U.S. National Arboretum reports that Black Pearl maintains its compact upright shape without pruning. Do not automatically apply pruning practices used for other pepper production goals to this ornamental cultivar.

flowering.short: Purple summer flowers precede upright ornamental fruit clusters
flowering.guidance: The National Arboretum describes summer-borne purple flowers that are not themselves ornamental, followed by upright clusters of 6–8 round fruits. Fruits begin glossy black and mature cherry red; the mature-fruit display is reported as lasting about 80–120 days, occasionally 140. This is cultivar-specific ornamental display information, not a harvest calendar.

propagation.short: The named cultivar is available as seed
propagation.guidance: USDA ARS reports seed availability for the named cultivar. The reviewed cultivar-release record does not give sowing depth, germination time or temperature; those details remain unverified here.

harvest.short: Fruit color transition is an ornamental cue
harvest.guidance: The USDA Arboretum introduction describes fruit emerging black and turning cherry red. It presents the cultivar for ornamental use; this profile does not infer that the fruits are intended for eating.

problems.short: Heat and uneven moisture can affect pepper flowering and fruit
problems.guidance: University of Minnesota Extension's guidance is for peppers at crop level, not specifically Black Pearl: hot days and nights can cause flower drop, while inconsistent soil moisture can weaken flowers and small fruit and contribute to blossom-end rot. Treat these as general Capsicum warning signs; cultivar-specific susceptibility or disease resistance has not been established.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Limited pot-culture/high-light evaluations do not establish hydroponic suitability.

growthHabits.reason: Cultivar-specific habit remains documented in sourced Plant Profile content; Compatibility Profile v1 does not encode cultivar-level evidence scope.

height.reason: Cultivar-specific dimensions remain in sourced Plant Profile content; Compatibility Profile v1 does not encode cultivar-level evidence scope.

name: White Carolina Pineberry
variety: Supplier-listed name 'White Carolina'; historical unpatented breeding parent documented, current retail-stock equivalence not established
summary: White Carolina is a supplier-listed pineberry name within Fragaria × ananassa. A US plant patent documents White Carolina as an unpatented white-fruited breeding parent, but does not authenticate current retail stock as the same clone. Pineberry-type fruit is pale when ripe; pollination claims for marketed White Carolina plants conflict.

identity.short: Supplier-listed name with a historical breeding record; retail stock not authenticated
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Fragaria × ananassa as the garden-strawberry hybrid. Ebert's Greenhouse and Raintree Nursery market White Carolina pineberry plants under that hybrid. US plant patent USPP34612 documents White Carolina/White Pine as an unpatented, white-fruited Fragaria × ananassa parent of QBC-1, supporting historical use of the name in strawberry breeding. It does not register White Carolina or prove that current nursery stocks are clonal matches to the patent's parent. The patent gives inconsistent USDA PI numbers in separate passages; neither is assigned here.

cultivation.short: Pineberry is a white-fruited garden-strawberry type
cultivation.guidance: University of Illinois Extension says pineberries can be grown like garden strawberries: full sun, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch to suppress weeds and moderate soil moisture and temperature. This is pineberry-type outdoor guidance, not a White Carolina-specific recipe or hydroponic recommendation.

growth.short: Pale-to-blush ripe fruit with red achenes; dimensions vary by cultivar
growth.guidance: Illinois Extension describes pineberry-type fruit as generally smaller and softer than standard red strawberries, with white-to-blush ripe color and red achenes. For the supplier-listed White Carolina selection, Ebert's and Walters Gardens each list 6–8 in height and 12–18 in spread; Raintree lists 6–10 in height and the same spread. These are supplier specifications, not independent trial measurements, and the catalog's current stock is not authenticated as the same clone, so they are not presented as a guaranteed mature size. Ebert also reports numerous runners; this has not been independently confirmed for the selection represented here.

harvest.short: Use achene color, not white flesh alone, as a ripeness cue
harvest.guidance: Illinois Extension describes ripe pineberries as white to blush with bright-red achenes; the achenes changing from green to red are a more reliable maturity cue than softness. Harvest gently with a twist or pinch. This is pineberry-type guidance, not a White Carolina-specific harvest date.

pollination.short: A compatible red-fruited strawberry is a cautious pollination partner
pollination.guidance: Illinois Extension recommends a compatible red-fruited garden cultivar for many pineberries and gives a type-level ratio of three pineberries to one standard strawberry. For its White Carolina product, Walters Gardens recommends one everbearing variety per five plants to help pollination and improve landscape performance. Raintree also recommends an everbearing partner at that ratio, although its listing calls White Carolina self-fertile; Ebert's says another strawberry's pollen is required. The sources therefore agree that a partner can help but do not agree whether it is required or establish one universal ratio. As a Garden adaptation while the stock represented here remains unauthenticated, grow a compatible everbearing red-fruited strawberry nearby if prioritizing fruit set; do not treat either ratio as a universal or verified compatibility rule for this catalog stock.

propagation.short: Buy pineberry plants, not seed, to retain the white-fruit type; stock identity remains unverified
propagation.guidance: University of Missouri Extension lists White Carolina among marketed pineberry cultivars and advises purchasing plants rather than seed to maintain white-fruit character. This is pineberry-type propagation guidance; it does not authenticate current White Carolina retail stock or supply a cultivar-specific vegetative propagation protocol. Ebert's product page reports numerous runners for its White Carolina listing, but no independent source reviewed here verifies that behavior for the selection represented in this catalog.

needsValidation.short: Supplier stocks are not authenticated as the historic line; pollination claims conflict
needsValidation.guidance: The patent documents a historical, unpatented White Carolina/White Pine breeding parent but does not authenticate current nursery stock as that same clone. Illinois Extension describes pineberries as self-sterile, and Ebert's says its White Carolina listing needs pollen from another strawberry. Raintree labels its listing self-fertile but still recommends one everbearing partner per five plants; Walters Gardens independently gives that same product-level recommendation. The practical value of a partner is supported, but whether the catalog's current stock strictly requires one remains unresolved. Ebert's runner report and seller size ranges remain product-page claims. The patent also prints different USDA PI numbers in separate passages, so no accession is assigned.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: General pineberry transplant guidance does not establish compatibility with a hydroponic system.

growthHabits.reason: The cultivar-specific plant habit was not established.
